title: Limits: brittleness and the knowledge bottleneck
text:
CHAPTER 12. EXPERT SYSTEMS
SECTION 12.3. LIMITS: BRITTLENESS AND THE KNOWLEDGE BOTTLENECK

Expert systems worked. XCON configured real computers, MYCIN matched specialists on test cases, and rule engines still run businesses. But the hope of the early 1980s, that most expert work could be automated by writing down experts' rules, failed. This section analyzes why, in technical terms: the knowledge acquisition bottleneck, brittleness, the difficulty of maintaining large rule bases, the logical problems of common-sense reasoning, and the philosophical critique that much expertise cannot be written down at all. It ends with the most ambitious attempt to overcome these limits by brute force, the Cyc project, and with how machine learning changed the problem.

1. The knowledge acquisition bottleneck

The central problem became known as the knowledge acquisition bottleneck, a term associated with Feigenbaum and his colleagues: getting knowledge into the machine was the slowest step. Knowledge engineering meant long interviews with experts, case reviews, building prototypes, and showing the experts the system's mistakes to elicit new rules. Typical difficulties:

  - Experts are busy and expensive.
  - Experts often cannot state their reasoning. Asked how they decide, they give plausible rules that do not match what they actually do, or say "it just looks wrong."
  - Knowledge is incomplete. Each new case uncovers exceptions.
  - Different experts disagree (as the MYCIN evaluation showed, Section 12.1).

The cost scales roughly with the number of rules, and the number of rules needed grows with the breadth of the domain. Building a system for one narrow task took person-years; building one for broad competence seemed to require effort beyond any project.

2. Tacit knowledge

The philosopher Michael Polanyi wrote in "The Tacit Dimension" (1966) that "we can know more than we can tell." Recognizing a face among thousands is the classic example: we do it reliably but cannot list the rules. Many expert skills, such as a physician's sense that a patient "looks sick," a technician hearing a bearing going bad, or a chess master's sense of a good position, have this character.

Hubert Dreyfus, a philosopher at MIT and later Berkeley, made the most sustained critique of AI on these grounds. Hired as a consultant by the RAND Corporation in 1964 to review Newell and Simon's work, he wrote the combative "Alchemy and Artificial Intelligence" (RAND paper, 1965) and later "What Computers Can't Do" (1972). Drawing on phenomenology (Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty), he argued that human expertise rests on embodied, situated, intuitive skill and background understanding that cannot be captured as explicit rules over symbols. With his brother Stuart Dreyfus he proposed a model of skill acquisition in which novices follow rules but experts no longer do; they perceive situations directly. If so, interviewing experts for rules extracts mainly the novice's version of their knowledge.

AI researchers at the time were often dismissive of Dreyfus, and some of his specific claims were overstated or misreported (he is often said to have predicted that computers would never play good chess, which is not what he wrote; he reported the state of the art of the time). But his central point, that much intelligence is tacit pattern recognition rather than explicit rule following, was largely vindicated, ironically by machine learning: neural networks acquire exactly this kind of tacit, unarticulated skill from examples.

3. Brittleness

Expert systems typically had a "cliff" at the edge of their competence. Inside the domain they did well. Just outside it they failed badly, and they did not know they were failing. Examples of the kind often cited (described generically): a medical system that, given data about a case outside its domain, confidently diagnoses within its narrow category; a car-loan system that approves a loan for an applicant who claims to have worked at a job for longer than they have been alive, because no rule checks that.

Reasons:

  - Rules cover the cases the designers anticipated. The world contains endless unanticipated cases.
  - Rules encode surface associations without the underlying causal model, so the system cannot reason from first principles when the rules run out.
  - There was no common sense to notice absurdity.
  - Systems had no measure of how far a case was from their experience.

Researchers tried to address this with "deep" models (causal and physical models of devices, qualitative physics, model-based diagnosis) alongside "shallow" heuristic rules. Model-based diagnosis, which reasons from a model of a device's components and connections to find which component faults explain observed symptoms, was a genuine success in engineering diagnosis and is used in some aerospace and automotive systems. It works when an accurate structural model is available, which is again a knowledge engineering cost.

Machine learning systems are also brittle under distribution shift (inputs unlike their training data), so this problem has not disappeared; it has changed form. A neural classifier can also be confidently wrong outside its training distribution. The modern response involves uncertainty estimation, out-of-distribution detection, and training on far broader data.

4. Maintenance and rule interactions

A rule base is a program, and a peculiar one: control flow is implicit in the conflict resolution strategy, so the effect of adding one rule can be hard to predict. With thousands of rules:

  - New rules can shadow or conflict with old ones.
  - Rules written by different engineers use inconsistent assumptions.
  - Knowledge changes (new products for XCON, new drugs for MYCIN) and must be updated continuously.
  - Testing is hard: the space of possible situations is huge.

DEC needed a substantial staff to maintain XCON, and by the early 1990s systems such as XCON were proving too expensive to maintain. Software engineering methods for rule bases (modularization into rule groups, verification tools that detect redundant, conflicting or unreachable rules, regression test suites of cases) helped, but did not remove the cost.

5. The logic of exceptions: frame, qualification and ramification

Common-sense reasoning exposed problems in the logic itself.

The frame problem (McCarthy and Hayes, 1969): when an action happens, how do we represent everything that does not change? In first-order logic, naive approaches need a "frame axiom" for every action and every fact it leaves unchanged: painting a block does not change its position, its weight, the color of other blocks, and so on. With A actions and F fluents (changeable facts), that is on the order of A * F axioms. Solutions include STRIPS-style delete lists (Section 9.4), and successor state axioms (Ray Reiter, 1991), which give, for each fluent, one axiom stating exactly when it becomes true or false, reducing the count to about F axioms.

The qualification problem: real rules have endless preconditions. "If you turn the key, the car starts," unless the battery is dead, there is no fuel, the starter is broken, there is a potato in the tailpipe, and so on. Listing all qualifications is impossible.

The ramification problem: actions have indirect effects. Moving a box moves everything inside it.

These led to nonmonotonic logics (around 1980): circumscription (McCarthy), default logic (Reiter), and others. In classical logic, adding premises never removes conclusions (monotonicity). In common sense, it does: "Tweety is a bird" suggests "Tweety flies"; adding "Tweety is a penguin" withdraws it. Default logic writes rules like

    bird(x) : flies(x) / flies(x)

meaning: if x is a bird and it is consistent to assume x flies, conclude x flies. These logics are mathematically rich, but reasoning in them is computationally harder than classical logic (often much harder in the worst case), and choosing the right defaults is itself a knowledge problem.

Probability offered a different answer. Instead of "birds fly, with exceptions," say P(flies | bird) = 0.9, P(flies | penguin) close to 0. Bayesian networks (Pearl, 1988) made such reasoning tractable in many cases (Chapter 14). Exceptions become conditioning on more evidence, which is natural in probability.

6. Cyc: common sense by hand

If brittleness came from lack of common sense, why not write common sense down? Douglas Lenat (1950-2023), known earlier for the discovery programs AM and Eurisko, started the Cyc project ("from encyclopedia") in July 1984 at MCC, the US research consortium formed partly in response to Japan's Fifth Generation project (Section 11.2). The goal was to encode the millions of facts and rules of everyday knowledge that people assume when they read an encyclopedia, so that later systems could build on them. Cyc later continued at the company Cycorp.

Cyc used a logic-based representation language, CycL, with an ontology of concepts organized into "microtheories" (contexts with their own assumptions), and inference engines with many specialized reasoning modules. In 1986 Lenat estimated that completing Cyc would take at least 250,000 rules and 1,000 person-years of effort, probably twice that. By later reports, the knowledge base contained on the order of a million assertions by 1994 and tens of millions by the late 2010s, mostly written by hand.

Cyc is the largest test of the hypothesis that common sense can be captured as explicit symbolic knowledge. Its results are debated. It was used in some applications (for example in commercial and government projects), and it is a major achievement of knowledge representation. But it did not produce the general-purpose common-sense reasoning that would have transformed AI, and it was overtaken in practice by statistical and neural methods that learn associations from huge amounts of text. Large language models (Chapter 19) absorb a broad, if imperfect and unstructured, form of common-sense knowledge from text without hand-coding: a striking reversal of Cyc's approach.

7. How machine learning changed the bottleneck

The response that eventually dominated was to learn knowledge from data instead of eliciting it from experts:

  - Rule learning: decision tree learners like ID3 (Quinlan, 1986) and C4.5 learned rules from labeled cases. Quinlan's work included an expert system for the interpretation of thyroid assays (1985). Learned trees often matched hand-built rules at a fraction of the effort.
  - Statistical classifiers and Bayesian networks learned probabilities from data (Chapter 14).
  - Neural networks learned tacit features directly from raw inputs (Chapters 13 and 16).

This moves the bottleneck from knowledge to data: labeled examples, which are often cheaper than expert interviews because they can be collected from normal operation (logged transactions, medical records, sensor data). Deep learning then moved it again, toward compute and enormous unlabeled datasets with self-supervised learning (Chapters 17-19).

What was lost: explicitness. A rule base can be read, explained and edited; a neural network's knowledge is distributed over millions or billions of weights. Explainability, auditability and the ability to insert known constraints are reasons rules survive in regulated domains and safety-critical engineering. Neurosymbolic AI, knowledge graphs combined with learned models, and LLMs calling explicit tools and rule checkers are current attempts to get both benefits.

8. Lessons for engineers

  - Explicit rules work well when the domain is narrow, stable, well understood, and the knowledge can be stated. Interlocks, safety logic and configuration constraints are good examples; write them as explicit, testable rules.
  - When the input is perceptual, noisy or open-ended (images, sound, vibration signatures, natural language), learned models usually beat hand-written rules.
  - In both cases, know where the system's competence ends. Check inputs for plausibility, detect out-of-range cases, and fail safe.
  - Plan for maintenance from the start: the cost of keeping knowledge current, whether rules or training data, often exceeds the cost of building the first version.

9. Summary

  - The knowledge acquisition bottleneck: eliciting rules from experts was slow, costly, incomplete and inconsistent.
  - Much expertise is tacit (Polanyi, 1966); Dreyfus (1965, 1972) argued that expert skill is not rule following, a view largely vindicated by machine learning.
  - Expert systems were brittle: competent inside a narrow domain, confidently wrong just outside it, without common sense or awareness of their limits.
  - Large rule bases were hard to maintain because rules interact implicitly.
  - The frame, qualification and ramification problems led to nonmonotonic logics; probability and Bayesian networks offered an alternative treatment of exceptions.
  - Cyc (Lenat, from 1984) tried to hand-code common sense at enormous scale; it was overtaken by learned approaches.
  - Machine learning moved the bottleneck from expert knowledge to data, at the cost of explicitness.
